conclusions.decision: No existing article or Academy lesson explains Britain's keep-left history. Existing calendar-change History piece concerns dates, not roads; a contextual link connects two distinct conventions.

No existing cat-box behaviour article or lesson. Cat references in anagrams and chunking are word examples; calendar boxes are number analogies, not hiding-box explanations. The current Curiosity nature/food questions cover different mechanisms.

checkedSources.type: UK Parliament first-party history of its road legislation
checkedSources.access: Complete relevant web page successfully opened. Direct download returned 403; a labelled excerpt of the relevant checked paragraph is archived instead.
checkedDetails: Parliament states the 1835 Act formalised the existing keep-left practice.
checkedSources.readScope: Complete short Parliamentary roads body read, especially Public legislation. Archive contains the relevant paragraph, not an HTML download.

checkedSources.access: Successful web open and direct source archive
checkedDetails: Keep-left origins are presented as possible, not established; the sword-arm explanation is treated cautiously.
Before enforcement, coach drivers leaving London could choose the firmest road surface.
checkedSources.readScope: Relevant keep-left question and context. Broad 1835 all-Britain-and-Ireland wording is not repeated; the original Act is specifically scoped to England.

checkedSources.access: Successful web open and direct source archive
checkedDetails: Section 78 (LXXVIII), printed pages 399–400, requires waggons, carts, carriages and animals meeting other traffic to keep left or near side.
Original title and scope identify highways in England.
checkedSources.readScope: Relevant original title/scope and section 78 checked in full; PDF pages 31–32 (one-based), with the keep-left text on PDF page 32 / printed page 400. Not a claim to have read every other provision or to give current legal advice.

checkedSources.type: Current Department for Transport Highway Code
checkedSources.access: Successful web open and direct source archive
checkedDetails: Rule 160 retains keeping left as the general instruction and explicitly provides exceptions.
checkedSources.readScope: Rule 160 opened and checked on 17 October 2026. No simplified universal driving instruction replaces its conditions.

checkedSources.access: Successful web open and direct source archive
checkedDetails: Published 14 October 2019; reported results for 23 Dutch shelter cats, 12 with boxes and 11 controls; 12-day behavioural observations.
Stress scores declined faster with hiding boxes. No significant between-group weight-loss difference.
checkedSources.readScope: Full article introduction, methods, results, discussion and conclusion checked. Methods also report two earlier exclusions; no total initial-enrolment number inferred. Posture/behaviour score is not a direct report of feelings. Small, individually housed shelter sample; no universal home-cat preference, cure, cortisol or adoption benefit claimed.

checkedSources.type: Original research abstract on authors' Utrecht University portal
checkedSources.access: Successful web open and direct source archive
checkedDetails: Abstract reports 19 newly arrived shelter cats randomly assigned, 10 with boxes and nine controls.
Box group improved earlier; average scores similar by day 14.
checkedSources.readScope: Complete original abstract only. Full article listed as embargoed until 2050 and not read. No claim based on inaccessible full text.

excludedOrLimitedSourceChecks.notes: Successful separate web access is recorded in checkedSources where applicable.

excludedOrLimitedSourceChecks.result: University portal explicitly lists full version under embargo until 2050. No claim to have read it and no bypass attempted.
excludedOrLimitedSourceChecks.notes: Public original abstract successfully read and archived; public article identifies that scope.

reading.limitations: The original 1835 Act is scoped to England; early keep-left origins are uncertain and modern rule 160 has exceptions. Small shelter studies support a hiding-space explanation without establishing universal home-cat preferences or preventing weight loss. The 2014 source is the original abstract, not inaccessible full text.
